meta.note: Good practices added for this page. Good practices from the IHR Benchmarks Good Practices page are reused through the crosswalk and shown with the benchmark they come from. Takeaways are one-line summaries in our own words, based on the abstract or page, not the full text. Ten sources were added on 2026-11-08 for indicators that had none of their own (abstracts read via Europe PMC).

sources.title: Evaluating implementation of International Health Regulations core capacities: using the Electronic States Parties Self-Assessment Annual Reporting Tool (e-SPAR) to monitor progress with Joint External Evaluation indicators
sources.authors: Razavi A, Collins S, Wilson A, Okereke E
sources.takeaway: Most SPAR indicators match JEE indicators closely, so SPAR can track progress between JEE missions, with gaps for AMR and immunisation.

sources.title: Epidemic preparedness and response capacity against infectious disease outbreaks in 186 countries, 2018–2022
sources.authors: Eze P, et al.
sources.takeaway: Analysis of SPAR data shows gains in five domains from 2018 to 2022, but many countries, especially in Africa, still lack functional capacity; self-reports may overstate it.

sources.title: An ecological study on the association between International Health Regulations (IHR) core capacity scores and the Universal Health Coverage (UHC) service coverage index
sources.authors: Lee Y, Kim S, Oh J, Lee S
sources.takeaway: Countries with higher IHR capacity scores tended to have higher service coverage, even after adjustment, suggesting health security and UHC reinforce each other.

sources.title: Belize enhances health security and emergency preparedness through the 2024 e-SPAR assessment and IHR core capacities workshop
sources.authors: PAHO/WHO
sources.takeaway: A multisectoral workshop (health, agriculture, environment and security, including civil aviation and the defence force) used the e-SPAR to find gaps that will inform a work plan, and agreed to reconvene after six months to review progress.
sources.note: Press release, not a study; it does not report results.

sources.title: Prioritization of zoonoses for multisectoral, One Health collaboration in Somalia, 2023
sources.authors: Osman AY, et al.
sources.takeaway: Human, animal, agriculture and environment sectors ranked 33 candidate zoonoses with a CDC tool and agreed seven priorities to guide joint surveillance, preparedness and workforce work.

sources.title: Outbreak of listeriosis in South Africa associated with processed meat
sources.authors: Thomas J, Govender N, McCarthy KM, et al.
sources.takeaway: Genome sequencing and a case-control study traced 937 cases to one factory's ready-to-eat meat; the recall was followed by a sharp drop in cases.

sources.title: South Africa's Listeria outbreak declared over: what lessons did we learn?
sources.authors: Rapid Microbiology (news)
sources.takeaway: The response exposed a fragmented food control system without mandatory HACCP or a legal limit for Listeria, prompting calls for a single food safety authority and new rules for ready-to-eat meat plants.
sources.note: Trade news summary; check against official outbreak reports.

sources.title: Country programme on food safety (Mongolia)
sources.authors: WHO Mongolia
sources.takeaway: Describes an emergency operations centre, a national food emergency response plan, a food laboratory network and an intersectoral strategy drafted with security and health agencies.
sources.note: WHO feature story; not independently evaluated.

sources.title: An evaluation of national capacity regarding chemical event management under the International Health Regulations: a case of Thailand, 2022
sources.authors: Praekunatham H, Boonmephong K
sources.takeaway: A JEE-based review found strong national and intermediate chemical event capacity but weak primary level and points of entry; it recommends an action plan and staff training.

sources.title: The radiological accident in Goiânia
sources.authors: IAEA
sources.takeaway: Classic case report on a stolen radiotherapy source: chronology, medical and remedial response, and recommendations.

sources.title: The international follow-up of individuals potentially exposed to polonium-210 in London 2006
sources.authors: Shaw K, Anders K, Olowokure B, et al.
sources.takeaway: The UK followed up 664 people abroad who may have been exposed and found few with meaningful contamination, showing how much cross-border cooperation such events need.

sources.title: Radiological incident: London, England
sources.authors: UK Government Decontamination Service
sources.takeaway: Describes how an operations centre, specialist contractors and multi-agency partners decontaminated nine venues after the polonium-210 poisoning.

sources.title: Evidence from 617 laboratories in 47 countries for SLMTA-driven improvement in quality management systems
sources.authors: Yao K, Luman ET, SLMTA Collaborating Authors
sources.takeaway: Shows a stepwise route to a working laboratory quality system before formal accreditation, with measurable gains across many countries.

sources.title: Willingness of WHO staff to work in health emergencies in the African Region: opportunity for phased deployment of staff and ensure continuity of health services
sources.authors: Gueye AS, Okeibunor J, Ngofa R, et al.
sources.takeaway: A volunteer surge roster is a quick way to find deployable staff, but planning has to account for gender balance, family duties and safety.

sources.title: National survey of Ebola-related knowledge, attitudes and practices before the outbreak peak in Sierra Leone: August 2014
sources.authors: Jalloh MF, Sengeh P, Monasch R, et al.
sources.takeaway: A rapid national KAP survey mid-epidemic found near-universal awareness but common misconceptions and stigma, giving community engagement a concrete target.

sources.title: Assessing the effectiveness of the integrated sample referral system in Tanzania: insights from a nationwide study
sources.authors: Torokaa PR, Ocheng D, Kelly ME, et al.
sources.takeaway: A national supervision tool applied to 97 sample referral hubs scored the system at about 64%, with financing weakest and lower-level hubs lagging, showing where to target support.

sources.title: Outbreak preparedness for women and girls in low- and middle-income countries: a qualitative study
sources.authors: Sarraf D, Meinhart M, Seff I, et al.
sources.takeaway: Experienced outbreak responders say gender and GBV risks are routinely dropped in emergencies and call for gender-balanced leadership, women-led partners and flexible funding.

sources.title: Tracking spending on prevention, preparedness and response to global health threats
sources.authors: OECD
sources.takeaway: Uses health accounts to track what countries spend on preparedness, showing lower-income countries rely mostly on external funds and are exposed to aid cuts.

sources.title: Exercise Crystal: simulations that drive National IHR Focal Point capacity-strengthening
sources.authors: Goddard L, Khut QY, Samaan G
sources.takeaway: Sixteen years of annual NFP simulation scores show email reach and WHO notification improved, while phone reachability and multisectoral communication still lag.

sources.title: Field epidemiology training in Tunisia: achievements and gaps
sources.authors: Charaa N, Letaief H, Chahed MK, et al.
sources.takeaway: Maps FETP graduates against the 1-per-200,000 target by governorate, finding most regions short and an ageing pool, and argues for career paths and domestic funding.

sources.title: Evaluation of the International Health Regulations core capacities at designated points of entry in Liberia, December 2019
sources.authors: Gray SLA, Nyenswah TG, Gilayeneh JSM, et al.
sources.journal: Journal of Interventional Epidemiology and Public Health 7:8
sources.takeaway: WHO checklist assessment of eight designated ports found trained staff and power in place but gaps in handwashing, communication equipment, isolation space and transport for ill travellers.
sources.note: No working DOI; links to the journal's article page.

sources.title: Health security capacities in the context of COVID-19 outbreak: an analysis of International Health Regulations annual report data from 182 countries
sources.authors: Kandel N, Chungong S, Omaar A, Xing J
sources.takeaway: Built prevent, detect, respond, enabling and readiness indices from 18 SPAR indicators (2018 data): 76% of countries scored highest on detection, and 32 had low operational readiness on the eve of COVID-19.

sources.title: Implementation of the 7-1-7 target for detection, notification, and response to public health threats in five countries: a retrospective, observational study
sources.authors: Bochner AF, Makumbi I, Aderinola O, et al.
sources.takeaway: Of 41 events, 54% met 7 days to detect, 71% 1 day to notify and 27% the full 7-1-7; most detection bottlenecks were at health facilities and notification and response delays at intermediate levels.

sources.title: COVID-19 and resilience of healthcare systems in ten countries
sources.authors: Arsenault C, Gage A, Kim MK, et al.
sources.takeaway: Interrupted time series of 31 services: every country saw disruptions, unrelated to income or pandemic intensity, and half still had substantial gaps at the end of 2020, a measure of what continuity plans must prevent.

sources.title: Evidence of the effectiveness of travel-related measures during the early phase of the COVID-19 pandemic: a rapid systematic review
sources.authors: Grépin KA, Ho TL, Liu Z, et al.
sources.takeaway: 29 studies, 26 of them models: early travel measures changed the first phase of the pandemic (Wuhan measures cut exported cases by 70–80%), but evidence outside China was scarce and timing mattered most.

sources.title: The first WHO global survey on infection prevention and control in health-care facilities
sources.authors: Tomczyk S, Twyman A, de Kraker MEA, et al.
sources.takeaway: IPCAF responses from 4,440 facilities: only 15% met all minimum requirements (none in low-income countries); staffing and training scored lowest, a checklist for where national IPC programmes need to invest.

sources.title: Prevalence of healthcare-associated infections, estimated incidence and composite antimicrobial resistance index in acute care hospitals and long-term care facilities: results from two European point prevalence surveys, 2016 to 2017
sources.authors: Suetens C, Latour K, Kärki T, et al.
sources.takeaway: Coordinated point prevalence surveys in 1,209 hospitals and 2,221 long-term care facilities found 6.5% and 3.9% of patients with an HAI: a model for national HCAI surveillance with validation.

sources.title: Emergency risk communication: lessons learned from a rapid review of recent gray literature on Ebola, Zika, and yellow fever
sources.authors: Toppenberg-Pejcic D, Noyes J, Allen T, et al.
sources.takeaway: Rapid review of 83 documents for WHO's risk communication guideline: lessons on community engagement, building trust and using social media during outbreaks.

sources.title: Travel and border health measures to prevent the international spread of Ebola
sources.authors: Cohen NJ, Brown CM, Alvarado-Ramy F, et al.
sources.takeaway: How exit screening in affected countries, enhanced entry risk assessment at US ports and traveller guidance were run during the 2014–2016 Ebola epidemic, and the partnerships that made it work.

sources.title: A scoping review of evaluation methods for health emergency preparedness exercises
sources.authors: Skryabina E, Riley P, Reedy G, Amlôt R
sources.takeaway: Across 64 studies, exercise evaluation methods were chosen without a guiding method; the authors advise matching methods to purpose and pairing participant feedback with objective performance data.

sources.title: Comparative analysis of national legislation in support of the revised International Health Regulations: potential models for implementation in the United States
sources.authors: Katz R, Kornblet S
sources.takeaway: Compares how four federal states put IHR obligations into national law when most public health powers sit at subnational level, offering models for countries with a similar structure.
